abstract: FOXG1 syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with communication impairment as a defining clinical feature, yet vocal behavior has not been characterized in animal models of FOXG1. We examined neonatal ultrasonic vocalizations in two mouse models that disrupt Foxg1 in distinct developmental and cellular contexts: a NEX-Cre-driven conditional heterozygous model targeting postmitotic cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons, and a W300X/+ knock-in model carrying a patient derived truncating mutation at the endogenous Foxg1 locus. Vocalizations were recorded at postnatal day 7 and analyzed for call number, duration, frequency range, and repertoire composition. The two models exhibited distinct vocal phenotypes. Conditional heterozygous mice produced longer calls while total vocal output, frequency range, and repertoire composition were preserved. In contrast, W300X/+ mice produced shorter calls, showed a significant shift in repertoire composition, and a non-significant trend toward reduced vocal output. The effect of genotype on call duration differed significantly between models, demonstrating opposing effects on temporal vocal structure. Frequency range was not significantly altered by genotype in either model, although sex was associated with frequency range in the conditional heterozygous cohort. These findings provide the first evidence that Foxg1 disruption alters neonatal vocal behavior and show that the resulting phenotype depends on the developmental, cellular, and molecular context of the mutation. Neonatal vocalizations therefore provide a sensitive behavioral readout for distinguishing functional consequences of disease relevant FOXG1 perturbations.
